scenes.narration: This picture shows three colored physical Direct Connect links entering one logical link aggregation group, or LAG. Start at the left endpoint and follow the cyan, purple, and yellow members into the transparent central cylinder. The group combines eligible dedicated connections using LACP and appears as one logical interface. That can simplify operations and increase available aggregate capacity. Now read the top-right warning: these members share a Direct Connect endpoint and its failure exposure. A LAG does not provide independence from a location-level outage. The lower-left box explains minimum active links. That threshold defines how many members must remain operational for the logical group to be considered active. Finally, the lower-right card shows multiple traffic flows distributed across member links. Aggregate bandwidth can increase, but a single flow is not guaranteed to achieve the sum of all member speeds. If the business requirement is more total traffic capacity at one endpoint, a LAG may fit. If the requirement is protection from a Direct Connect location failure, use a separately designed diverse connection instead.

scenes.narration: This is a failure-mode design slide, and each numbered panel defines one condition of successful recovery. In the first panel, choose an independent secondary Direct Connect path or a Site-to-Site VPN over the internet according to the required failure diversity and security. A backup must not rely on the same broken device or carrier path. Next, the route-sign illustration warns that backup route selection is not automatic just because two paths exist. Advertise and prefer prefixes deliberately, because a more-specific route can defeat the intended primary and backup ordering. In the third panel, the capacity gauge highlights a practical tradeoff. The backup need not always carry every noncritical transfer, but it must carry the prioritized critical workloads within the recovery objective. You may need throttling or queuing during degraded operation. Finally, the checklist calls for real failover tests: measure BGP or static route convergence, application reconnection, and time to useful recovery. A link showing healthy after convergence does not prove existing sessions survived. This slide teaches us to design a predictable, measurable degraded mode instead of assuming a second cable is enough.

scenes.narration: This slide compares four security boundaries rather than four interchangeable encryption products. Start at the left with TLS. It protects application sessions between the negotiated TLS endpoints, such as a client and a server or terminating proxy. Move to the purple panel: IPsec protects network traffic between VPN tunnel endpoints. It can provide encrypted connectivity over an otherwise untrusted transport, but does not automatically mean application end-to-end encryption beyond those endpoints. The next cyan panel shows MACsec. It protects a supported Layer Two point-to-point link, and its coverage ends at that link boundary. It is not the same as TLS between applications. Finally, the orange panel explicitly states that AWS Direct Connect traffic is not encrypted by default simply because it travels on private transport. If compliance requires protection across a particular segment, select an appropriate supported encryption layer for that segment. A design may deliberately combine TLS with IPSec or other protection when its trust boundaries demand it. The key question is not only whether traffic is encrypted, but between precisely which endpoints.

scenes.narration: This architecture layers an encrypted VPN on private hybrid transport. Follow the left-to-right path from the on-premises network through Direct Connect, a transit virtual interface, Direct Connect gateway, and Transit Gateway. These components provide the private underlay network. Above that, the purple tunnel and shield represent Site-to-Site VPN with private-IP endpoints, where IPsec encrypts the application traffic carried inside the overlay. The upper-right panel makes the security distinction clear: the VPN endpoints use private addresses while the protected traffic travels within the tunnel. Now inspect the two stacked routing layers in the bottom-left diagram. The underlay must make the VPN endpoint addresses reachable across private transport. The overlay advertises and routes the actual application prefixes through the encrypted tunnels. If those two route domains are mixed incorrectly, recursive routing or unintended bypass can occur. The final panel reminds us to verify supported service combinations, usable VPN capacity, and the failover behavior of both underlay and overlay. For a professional exam scenario, choose private IP VPN when an encrypted overlay is needed while preserving a privately carried transport path, then verify the entire chain.
